newsitem.title: USA: Texaco annual meeting hit with protests.
newsitem.headline: Texaco annual meeting hit with protests.

text.p: Texaco Inc's annual shareholder meeting on Tuesday was a magnet for those disenchanted with the company's attitudes on racial minorities, the environment and its investment in Burma.

Shareholders of the White Plains, N.Y., oil company were treated to banners and placards calling Texaco "The star destoyer of the forests," referring to the company logo and its alleged pollution of the rainforest in Ecuador.
"The oil they spilled is lying in pools in the forests. Texaco had the technology to clean the spills up, but did not use it," charged James Hansen of the Rainforest Action Group.

Texaco denies it caused pollution and recently won the first round of a billion dollar claim in the New York courts, which the environmentalists and the government of Ecuador have submitted for reconsideration.
Among the 40 protestors gathered outside the Rye Hilton, the Reverend Jesse Jackson's Rainbow-Push coalition demanded more women and minorities in management.

A shareholder motion submitted by the Evangelical Lutheran Church, which owns 3,200 shares of the oil giant, referred to Texaco's settlement last year of a racial discrimination lawsuit for $115 million plus an 11.4 percent increase in salaries for plaintiffs.
"We believe the judgments and perspectives of a more diverse board would improve the quality of corporate decision- making," the church said, demanding a report by September.

Texaco, which settled the 1996 suit rather than continue litigation after transcripts of tape recordings showed executives allegedly discussing the destruction of documents and making racist remarks, rejected the call.
The company said it had implemented a program to ensure fairness in the treatment of ethnic minorities and women.

"Arbitrary deadlines could sacrifice the thoroughess of this effort. All of this activity occurs of necessity behind the scenes, where the level and intensity of the effort cannot be apparent to stockholders," Texaco said in response.

Protestors are also angry that Texaco has not divested its 43 percent stake in a natural gas field in the Andaman Sea, off the coast of Burma, which they say is giving succor to Burma's military government.

Texaco shareholders overwhelmingly rejected a call to get out of Burma last year and the company has always said it will obey U.S. law, which was recently changed to halt new, but not existing, investment in Burma.
